summary: Lists short-term requirements for how trusted SIP network nodes pass along a Network Asserted Identity, which is an identity a network intermediary derives after authenticating a user. Unlike a self-chosen alias, it is vouched for by the network. The scope is trusted, securely interconnected networks.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3324 describes how a SIP network can establish an identity after checking a user and share it with trusted network nodes. The identity is reliable only within the secure relationships and agreed rules described by the RFC.

questions: what are the requirements for sip asserted identity
what is a sip trust domain
how does a network assert a sip identity
when must an asserted identity be ignored
subtitle: Requirements for trusted SIP networks to share an identity established after user authentication.

tldr.problem: A SIP user can put a chosen identity in a message, and another user agent may not have the information needed to authenticate it. The RFC sets requirements for a network to establish and share an identity it can vouch for.
tldr.mechanism: A network intermediary derives an identity after authenticating a user. Nodes exchange it over secure connections only when the receiving node is configured to trust the sender.
tldr.outcome: The requirements cover exchange and privacy within a defined Trust Domain and with directly connected trusted parties. They do not define a general identity system for arbitrary Internet hosts.

today: RFC 3324 is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the text limits these requirements to trusted, securely interconnected networks.

sections.title: Why Networks Assert an Identity
sections.content:
SIP messages can contain an identity chosen by the user, such as the value in the From: header. The RFC notes that this value is not required to be more than the user's preferred alias, and user agents may lack the key information needed to authenticate one another.

A Network Asserted Identity is an identity derived by a SIP network intermediary after an authentication process. RFC 3324 sets short-term requirements for exchanging that identity among securely connected, trusted nodes and user agents. General transport of asserted identities across the Internet is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A name in a SIP message may be only the name its sender chose. A network can establish a stronger identity by authenticating the user before it asserts one.

sections.title: Identities and Trust Domains
sections.content:
The identity is a sip:, sips:, or tel: URI, with an optional display name. Its URI must identify a domain or telephone-number owner that can route a request to the associated user or line; for a Network Asserted Identity, that domain or number owner must be within the Trust Domain.

A Trust Domain is a set of SIP nodes that follow shared handling rules, called Spec(T). A node is trusted by another node only when they have a secure connection and the receiving node is configured to recognize the sender as a member. The agreed rules cover how identities are generated, handled, and protected.
sections.plainLanguage: A Trust Domain is a group of SIP nodes that agree on how to handle asserted identities. A receiver trusts a sender only when their connection is secure and its configuration recognizes that sender.

sections.title: Generating and Exchanging an Identity
sections.content:
A network intermediary creates the asserted identity after authenticating the user agent. The authentication method and its strength are features of the Trust Domain's agreed rules. A user agent may provide a preferred identity, which the network may use according to its policy.

A node must be able to exchange an identity securely with another node it trusts. A trusted node may also send the identity to an outside node that trusts it, if the user's and domain's privacy rules allow. The identity identifies the originator of the message carrying it: for example, the caller in an initial INVITE and the answering party in a 200 response.

Multiple identities for one party may be carried when they use distinct supported URI types. A receiving node must not use an identity received from a node it does not trust, because the sender and integrity of that information are not assured.
sections.plainLanguage: The network creates the identity after authenticating the user, then shares it only across trusted secure connections. A receiver must ignore an identity from a sender it does not trust.

sections.title: Keeping an Identity Private
sections.content:
A message must be able to indicate that an asserted identity must not be passed to other users, without stating the reason. It must also be possible to indicate specifically that the user requested this privacy; the two indications can be equivalent under one Trust Domain's policy and different under another's.

When an identity is private, a trusted node must not send it to a node outside the set of parties it trusts. The identity may still be transferred within the trusted network. The RFC notes that a user's request for anonymity may require additional functions outside this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can say that an identity must not be shared outside trusted parties. It can also record that the user asked for privacy, without revealing why.

sections.title: Security Boundaries
sections.content:
RFC 3324 is not a general mechanism for arbitrary Internet hosts. It assumes a community whose nodes follow agreed rules and communicate over secure connections; those rules must define how an identity is authenticated and protected as it moves through the network.

Outside that setting, the RFC warns there is no guarantee that identity information is correct or has not been modified. It also states that the document has no IANA implications.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements depend on secure connections and trusted nodes that follow shared rules. Outside that setting, an asserted identity may be false or altered.

references.text: Rosenberg, J., et al., "SIP: Session Initiation Protocol", RFC 3261, June 2002.
